notes.b: Each household group needs a different combination of space, location, access and services.
points: Families need enough bedrooms for every member, adequate storage, a well-equipped and ventilated kitchen, and a living room for relaxing and watching television.
Families with young children need a safe, enclosed back garden; families with a car or sports equipment may need a garage or shed.
Single people usually need smaller, affordable accommodation close to work, college or public transport, with space for study.
Older people need single-storey living or a stairlift, level entrances, a home that is warm and easy to heat, and nearness to shops, health services and community facilities.

People with disabilities need adjustments that depend on the disability: ramps for wheelchair or walking-aid users, lowered switches and sockets, flashing lights linked to doorbells and alarms for people with a hearing disability, and an accessible bathroom.
Homeless people need emergency shelter in hostels or emergency bed and breakfast accommodation, followed by rent-assisted private accommodation and then a permanent home.
Local authority housing is rented housing allocated by need, with priority given to households unable to house themselves.
Allocation by local authorities considers household size, income, current accommodation, age and disability, and families, people with disabilities and older people are often given priority.
Voluntary housing is provided by approved housing bodies and voluntary organisations, often for specific groups such as older people, people with disabilities or homeless people.

Co-operative housing is built by a group of members who pool the costs of the site, builder and solicitor, and a local authority may provide a low-cost site for a co-operative whose members are on its waiting list.

Shared equity and affordable purchase: under the First Home scheme the State and participating lenders take an equity share in a new home, which the buyer can buy out later; local authorities also sell affordable homes below market price.
Demand for social housing exceeds supply, so applicants can wait for a number of years for a home.
Owner-occupation is the largest tenure in Ireland, followed by private renting and social housing.
Urban areas have higher density, more apartments and greater demand, while rural areas have one-off houses and, in some places, vacant homes.
Private housing is built by developers and sold or let on the open market; social housing is built and allocated by local authorities and approved housing bodies.
Strong demand in cities and commuter areas pushes up prices and rents, while some rural areas have vacant housing but fewer jobs and services.

notes.h: Quality of accommodation and comparative costs (Higher Level only)
points: A BER certificate rates a home's energy efficiency from A, the most efficient, to G, the least efficient.
Older housing stock is often poorly insulated and costly to heat, which can cause fuel poverty.
Damp, poor ventilation and inadequate lighting reduce the quality of accommodation and can affect health.
Buying involves a deposit, mortgage repayments and maintenance, and builds equity; renting involves rent with no return but lower upfront costs.
In high-demand urban areas, rent can be as high as, or higher than, mortgage repayments, but buying requires a deposit that many people cannot save.
Rural homes are often cheaper to buy than urban ones, but residents may have to travel further to reach schools, shops and jobs.

notes.h: Adequacy of housing provision (Higher Level only)
points: Adequacy means more than the number of dwellings: housing must be affordable, secure, suitable, accessible and near employment, transport, schools, healthcare and shops.
Low-income families, lone parents, homeless people, older people and people with disabilities may not get housing suited to their needs.
Emergency accommodation does not offer the stability of a permanent home.
Local authority building, voluntary and co-operative schemes increase supply, and adaptation grants help particular groups to stay in their homes.
Renovating vacant property and planning mixed, serviced developments are further ways to improve adequacy.
Schools, childcare and playgrounds serve children and reduce long journeys for families.
Shops, post offices, banks and community centres provide necessities and social contact.
Public transport gives access to employment and services; a development without transport isolates its residents.
Parks, sports grounds and play areas promote exercise, leisure and community interaction.
Street lighting improves safety, and regular refuse collection keeps the area hygienic.
Accessible healthcare, pharmacies and services for older people or people with disabilities support independence.
Setting: a group housing study of a local area such as a townland, village or housing estate, recording which amenities are present and which are missing.

keyTerms.definition: Housing provided at subsidised rents or costs for households in need, through local authorities, approved housing bodies or co-operatives.
A household that owns the home it lives in and is paying off a mortgage on it or has paid it off.
Housing built and managed by a group of members who pool their resources to share the costs of site, builder and professional services.
A scheme, such as First Home, in which the State and lenders own a share of a new home alongside the buyer, who can buy out that share later.
A situation in which a household cannot afford to heat its home adequately, often because of poor insulation or outdated heating.
The extent to which housing supply meets the needs of different groups in terms of affordability, suitability, accessibility and location.
Temporary shelter, such as a hostel or emergency bed and breakfast, provided to people who have no home.
Facilities such as schools, shops, transport, parks and healthcare that make a housing development a place to live.
A non-profit body approved to provide social housing, often for particular groups such as older people or people with disabilities.

factCards.term: Three ways a family's housing needs differ from a single person's
factCards.definition: More bedrooms and storage; a safe enclosed garden for young children; space for a car or sports equipment.

factCards.term: Four home adjustments for people with disabilities
factCards.definition: Ramps for wheelchair or walking-aid users; lowered switches and sockets; flashing visual alarms; an accessible bathroom.
Local authority housing; voluntary housing provided by approved housing bodies; co-operative housing built by a group of members.

factCards.term: Four facilities a new housing development should provide
factCards.definition: Schools and childcare; shops and services; public transport; play areas and parks.

factCards.term: Two reasons older housing can be costly to heat
factCards.definition: Poor insulation and draughts; outdated or inefficient heating systems.

factCards.term: Stage of homelessness support that follows emergency shelter
factCards.definition: Rent-assisted private accommodation, leading on to a permanent home.

questions.prompt: Name and describe two features a home should have to meet the needs of an older person living alone.
questions.model: Single-storey living or a stairlift, so that the person can reach all rooms safely without climbing stairs; level or ramped entrances and step-free access; a home that is warm and easy to heat, with good insulation; a location close to shops, health services and public transport. Any two features, each named and described, earn the marks.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the adequacy of housing provision in Ireland today for families, single people and homeless people.
questions.model: Adequacy means affordable, secure, suitable, accessible and well located housing. Families: adequate space, bedrooms and storage, and safe outdoor space; provision is limited in cities where large family homes are scarce and expensive. Single people: smaller, affordable accommodation such as apartments and private rented homes is available in urban areas, but rents are high and shared accommodation can be poor quality. Homeless people: emergency accommodation such as hostels and emergency bed and breakfast provides shelter but not the stability of a home; move-on supports such as rent-assisted private accommodation help some people, but long social housing waiting lists and the limited supply of permanent homes leave many in emergency accommodation. Overall distribution: strong demand in cities and commuter areas and vacancy in some rural areas; social provision by local authorities, approved housing bodies and co-operatives helps, but supply does not meet demand. Quality: older stock is costly to heat and may be damp, so some homes are not adequate. A balanced evaluation should reach a conclusion on which groups are best and worst served.
